newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN calls off meeting on Zaire; signs of progress.
newsitem.headline: UN calls off meeting on Zaire; signs of progress.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council called off a planned appeal to rebels for a truce in Zaire, with members saying there were signs of progress over the weekend that a public statement might endanger.

"We're keeping our powder dry for the moment and don't want to block anyone in the corners when things might be on the verge of moving," said one member in reference to U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun's ongoing negotiations in the region.

As rebels forces appeared to be closing in on Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city, the council had scheduled a statement at a public meeting late on Friday. But its current president, Zbigniew Wlosowicz of Poland, said members had changed their mind because of some positive signs.
Sahnoun, in Kigali, plans talks with Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu and Vice-President Maj-Gen Paul Kagame in his quest to forge a ceasefire in eastern Zaire, U.N. officials said.

He met Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Thursday in the northern Ugandan town of Gulu at a meeting arranged by Uganda President Yoweri Museveni. But Kabila has refused to agree to a ceasefire before negotiations on Zaire's future.
Diplomats said Sahnoun might return to Uganda over the weekend to meet Kabila again or go to Burundi before his planned visit to Nairobi to meet President Daniel arap Moi.

Both the United States and Britain have asked Uganda and Rwanda to use their influence with Kabila, diplomats said. The messages to leaders in the two countries so far have resulted in the Thursday meeting between Sahnoun and Kabila.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan warned Security Council members on Friday of the dangerous situation around Ubundi on the eatern bank of the Zaire River where more than 100,000 weakened Rwanda Hutu refugees have fled.
Aid officials fear that they will become a target of the rebels, particularly the young men of military age among them.
Annan, who had been unsuccessful in getting a military force to protect the refugees, has for the past week emphasised some kind of monitoring or peacekeeping after a ceasefire is reached.
France has revived efforts to rally an international force but the United States and Britain, among others, have resisted.
His spokesman Fred Eckhard said Annan told the council he wanted a "package of measures" implemented in three phases:
-- facilitating access and immediate humanitarian assistance to the refugees and displaced persons and safe repatriation of the refugees to Rwanda.
-- verifying the withdrawal of all foreign forces

Many of the refugees are hostage to Hutu militia and ex-soldiers who led 1994's genocide of minority Tutsis and cannot go back peacefully to Rwanda where a Tutsi-dominated army holds sway. The militia at times fought against the rebels and on the side of Zairean regular soldiers.

At stake in the forthcoming days is the battle for Kisangani, the nerve centre of Zairean military operations in the eastern Zaire. Kabila's forces, who have racked up a string of military successes, are often welcomed by the local poulation because of resentment against President Mobutu Sese Seko for driving a resource-rich nation into poverty.
At the same time there are widespread fears from all Western nations that a continuing civil war or even the breakup of Zaire would destabilise at least five of its neighbours.
